author: hlntnr
text: That's all, for real this time. Many thanks to the colleagues & friends who helped make this paper better! Many of them are sadly twitterless, but shoutout to @timhwang & @v_maini. And of course, most of the credit here goes to lead author Zach - was super fun working with him.

author: hlntnr
text: *OK, not quite lastly, because if I'm talking about accidental & structural risks then I definitely also have to shout out @r_zwetsloot & @AllanDafoe's great piece on that: https://t.co/yZ7tjmFMjd

author: hlntnr
text:
Lastly*, I want to call out the excellent "Technology Roulette," which was an inspiration for this paper. 

Richard makes the crucial point that tech superiority ≠ tech security. We have to take accidental & structural risks of tech progress seriously.
https://t.co/XU8jSCpBFf

author: hlntnr
text:
There's much more to say, but hopefully that's enough to pique your interest to read the paper. I'm really excited for CSET to be doing more work on AI accidents, safety, testing & evaluation, etc. 

If you're interested in this topic, we're hiring!
https://t.co/SvNEiy4C7J

author: hlntnr
text: Govts already track aviation and cyber incidents. Given how general-purpose AI is, this kind of monitoring will be critical if our regulatory/policy environment is going to have any chance of keeping up with how these systems are working (and not working) in reality.

author: hlntnr
text: Then we wrap up with, of course, our policy recommendations. Funding AI safety research is in there, of course, but a more novel rec that I'm excited about is for governments to follow the lead of https://t.co/gFzAgVQf7y and start tracking what causes AI accidents in the wild.

author: hlntnr
text: We also point out risk factors that make failures especially likely, including competitive pressure (Boeing 737 MAX...), system complexity or speed, untrained/distracted users, and systems where one model is used in lots of places (e.g. Tesla autopilot in millions of cars).

author: hlntnr
text:
We tell these stories in terms of three ways AI systems tend to fail - due to problems of robustness, specification, and assurance.

(big props to @v_maini and his team for this breakdown, and also for his super helpful review of this paper 🙏) https://t.co/dN7yoBrcSB

author: hlntnr
text:
To do that, we came up with a dozen vignettes of fictional AI accidents, which draw heavily on things that have already happened (e.g. remember this? ⬇️) but imagine more widespread and slightly more capable AI. 

https://t.co/Ln7CdU8IJD

quoted.text: This was so foreseeable that I literally have a draft paper in the works right now that uses "skin diagnosis app that fails on non-white people" as one of our hypothetical future scenarios. And yet Google still, somehow, did not foresee it.

author: hlntnr
text: Our goal was to combine what we know from past technological accidents—like oil spills/chemical leaks/etc—with what we know about how machine learning tends to fail, and paint a picture of the kinds of disasters we might see if AI keeps being rolled out rapidly into new sectors.

@picklepikkl @KelseyTuoc Yeah, part of what frustrates me here is that the coverage seems to be going for a generic "oh no, things are chaotic!" rather than trying to identify what the current & foreseeable bottlenecks are. 

Part of the problem is prob also that headline writers ≠ article writers.

author: hlntnr
text: The more shots we get in arms, the sooner we get the pandemic under control. Headlines of "hospitals are running out, oh no" lead the reader to conclude that hospitals should be retaining doses, rather than pointing at the actual bottleneck: federal supply & state distro. 3/3

author: hlntnr
text: This is a race between (very roughly) 3 groups: 1) the federal government, 2) state governments, and the 3) providers actually giving vaccinations. Each group should be racing as fast as it can *not to be the bottleneck*. Hospitals running out of vaccine = group 3 is winning. 2/3
